title: The Dutch Clothing Mountain: What Makes Consumers Keep Wearing Certain Clothes Again & Again?
description: Read article about This article analyses Dutch wardrobe data to show why comfort, fit, versatility, digital buying, and circular policy shape repeated clothing use in the Netherlands. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Dutch apparel consumption is less about purchase volume than under-use, with wardrobe evidence showing that comfort, fit, versatility, and occasion value determine whether garments are worn again.
Digital commerce, sportswear crossover, and circular policy make the Netherlands a useful case for linking marketing, product design, sourcing, repair, resale, and retention.
markdown:
The real question is not how much Dutch consumers buy. It is why some garments become part of their lives while others remain unworn.

Fashion consumption is usually measured through sales, spending, market size and purchase frequency. But a garment's commercial life does not end at purchase.

It begins there.

A consumer buys a garment, decides whether it feels right, wears it for different occasions, keeps or discards it, perhaps repairs or resells it, and eventually determines how long that product remains in use.

This makes one question particularly important for fashion businesses: What makes consumers wear a garment again?

Being a part of Global North, the Netherlands offers an interesting setting to explore this question. It combines a digitally mature consumer market, substantial international apparel trade, an established fashion culture and increasingly formal circular-textile policy. Yet recent Dutch wardrobe research also reveals a striking contradiction: consumers own substantial quantities of clothing, while a significant proportion is never worn.

The issue, therefore, may not be consumption alone. It may be under-use.

A Market that Buys, Imports, and Moves Fashion at Scale

The Netherlands has more than 18 million residents, but its importance to fashion extends well beyond its population.

The country imported approximately €17.9 billion of apparel in 2024, equivalent to around 3.1 billion units. It was the fourth-largest apparel importer in the EU by value. More than 60 per cent of its apparel imports by value came from developing countries, while India accounted for approximately 3.3 per cent of import value.

The country is also an important European distribution hub. The Port of Rotterdam and its wider logistics infrastructure allow products to enter the Netherlands and move onwards into other European markets. CBI (the Centre for the Promotion of Imports from developing countries) notes that the Netherlands re-exports around 90 per cent of the apparel value it imports.

This distinction matters.

Dutch apparel imports should not simply be interpreted as Dutch consumers personally purchasing €17.9 billion worth of clothing. A considerable proportion reflects the country's role as a gateway into Europe.

For fashion companies, however, the combination remains strategically important:

consumer market + digital commerce + logistics hub + circular-policy environment.

Inside the Dutch Wardrobe

The most useful recent evidence comes from the National Wardrobe Audit 20251, conducted by Hogeschool Rotterdam and partner institutions.

The study inventoried 958 Dutch wardrobes among people aged 15 to 70. It focused on clothing and excluded socks, underwear and shoes. The average wardrobe contained 125 garments.

For women, the average was 148 garments, compared with 102 for men. Around 9 per cent of garments were second-hand, while approximately one in six garments was never worn, even when it was suitable for the season.

This gives the traditional idea of the “clothing mountain” a different meaning.

It is not only:

How much clothing enters the wardrobe?

It is also:

How much of that clothing actually becomes useful?

The Wardrobe Journey:

Purchase → Ownership → First wear → Repeated wear → Repair / resale / reuse → Disposal

The biggest opportunity may therefore sit between ownership and repeated use.

The Garment People Love is not Necessarily the Garment Marketers Think they are Selling

One of the most revealing findings from the 2025 audit concerns favourite garments.

When consumers identified why a particular garment was a favourite, comfort and good fit accounted for 43.3 per cent of responses.

That was followed by:

| Reason | Share |
| Comfort and good fit | 43.3% |
| Looks and style | 16.6% |
| Versatility | 15.4% |
| Material and quality | 6.8% |
| Personal, unique or brand value | 6.4% |
| Emotional or sentimental value | 3.2% |
| Occasion suitability | 3.1% |
| Sustainability | 1.3% |

The finding does not suggest that Dutch consumers do not care about sustainability.

It suggests something more useful for business.

Consumers may value sustainability, but they experience the garment through comfort, fit, appearance, versatility and use.

This raises an interesting proposition:

Could Comfort be a Hidden Driver of Sustainability?

It would be premature to claim that comfort automatically creates longer garment life.

But the relationship is worth testing.

A garment that fits well, feels comfortable and works across different situations may be more likely to be worn repeatedly.

That creates a possible chain:

Comfort → attachment → repeated use → longer retention → potentially fewer replacements

If the fashion industry wants consumers to consume more responsibly, it may therefore need to understand not only why people buy, but why they keep choosing the same garment.

One Consumer can Represent Several Clothing Markets

A major limitation of demographic segmentation is that it treats a person as one consumer.

In reality, the same person may need different clothing for:

work → exercise → travel → friends → nightlife → dating → formal occasions → private life

The garment's value changes with the situation.

A pair of trousers may be valuable because it is professional at work.

The same person's sportswear may be valuable because it provides movement and comfort.

A particular outfit for a date may be chosen because it creates confidence or communicates identity.

A garment worn privately may be selected primarily for comfort, fit or personal confidence.

This suggests that clothing consumption should also be studied as situational consumption.

Research on dress and social impression has shown that clothing can communicate information about attractiveness, identity and social signalling. At the same time, the meaning assigned by an observer does not necessarily represent the wearer's intention.

The important commercial question is therefore not simply:

What clothes make someone attractive?

It is:

How does the purpose of the occasion change what the consumer wants from clothing?

The Missing Wardrobe

There is another important limitation in the current Dutch data.

The National Wardrobe Audit excluded underwear, socks and shoes.

This creates an interesting research gap.

Outerwear and everyday garments are relatively visible parts of consumption. Intimate apparel represents a different relationship with clothing.

A future study could examine whether consumers choose intimate garments primarily for:

Comfort, fit, confidence, personal identity, partner perception, sensuality, novelty, durability, or sustainability

The point is not to assume the answer.

The point is that the private wardrobe may operate according to different consumption logic from the public wardrobe.

That distinction deserves more research.

The Digital Wardrobe Starts Before the Physical Wardrobe

The Dutch consumer is also highly connected to digital commerce.

CBS reported that in 2024, 80.8 per cent of Dutch people aged 12 and above had made an online purchase, while clothing, footwear and accessories remained the most frequently purchased online product category, bought by approximately 59 per cent of people aged 12 and above.

This changes the traditional fashion journey.

Traditional Journey

Store → Product → Trial → Purchase

Digital Journey

Screen → Discovery → Comparison → Reviews → Recommendation → Purchase → Delivery → Wardrobe

Fashion discovery can now occur through:

social media, creators, search, marketplaces, brand websites, streaming content, recommendations, customer reviews and AI.

For fashion companies, this creates a direct connection between marketing and sourcing.

If digital content creates demand faster than conventional retail planning can respond, businesses need greater flexibility in:

initial production quantities + demand sensing + replenishment + lead times + supplier responsiveness.

The digital consumer is therefore also a supply-chain challenge.

When Sport Becomes Everyday Fashion

The boundary between sportswear and everydaywear is becoming increasingly fluid.

Current market research identifies active lifestyles and demand for comfort as important drivers of sportswear in the Netherlands.

A consumer may purchase a technical jacket, sweatshirt, sneaker or performance trouser for sport and then use it for commuting, travel, shopping or socialising.

The product moves through:

Performance → Comfort → Lifestyle → Identity

This is why the more useful question may be:

How many situations can this product serve?

rather than:

“Is this sportswear or fashion?”

That question also connects back to the wardrobe audit, where versatility was the third-largest reason a garment was identified as a favourite.

Dutch Fashion is Practical, but Not Predictable

The Dutch market is often associated with practical, functional and understated clothing.

CBI describes the market as having demand for comfortable and versatile garments, simple designs, easy-care fabrics and layering, supported by the country's temperate climate.

But practicality should not be confused with uniformity.

The Netherlands also has internationally recognised experimental and independent fashion voices, from designers such as Iris van Herpen and Viktor & Rolf to streetwear names including Daily Paper, Patta and Filling Pieces.

The better description is therefore:

Functionality + individuality

rather than simply:

Minimalism

The consumer can want comfort and practicality while simultaneously using clothing to express identity, creativity, culture and lifestyle.

Media can Shape Taste, but Causality Needs Evidence

Fashion is increasingly consumed through screens before it reaches the wardrobe.

Streaming, music, influencers, sport and entertainment provide visual references for how people dress and how lifestyles are represented.

The launch of Love Is Blind: Netherlands in September 2026 provides a timely example of a global entertainment format being localised for a Dutch audience.

For fashion research, dating formats are particularly interesting because they place clothing, appearance, identity and social impression into a visible environment.

But an important distinction must be made.

It would be easy to say:

“People saw an outfit on Netflix and bought it.”

Without search, sales or consumer data, that is an assumption.

The better question is:

Does repeated exposure to a fashion aesthetic through entertainment influence recognition, search, purchase intention or actual purchase?

That relationship can be measured.

Sustainability: From Consumer Preference to Business System

The Netherlands has also moved sustainability beyond voluntary brand communication.

Extended Producer Responsibility for textiles became operational in 2023, placing responsibilities on producers around collection, reuse and recycling. The Dutch government has also established a Circular Textile Programme for 2025–2030 as part of the longer-term transition towards a circular textile chain.

This changes the role of the fashion company.

Circularity is no longer only:

“Will consumers prefer sustainable fashion?”

It increasingly becomes:

“Can the company design, source, sell, collect, reuse and recycle products within a more circular system?”

Yet the wardrobe evidence shows that sustainability intention and actual use are not the same thing.

The 2025 audit found that approximately one in six garments was never worn. Among discarded garments, the leading reasons included:

•   31 per cent no longer fitting

•   28 per cent being worn out

•   21 per cent no longer being liked

•   The implication is important.

A sustainable garment that is never worn still represents a poor use of resources.

This is why retention deserves to become part of the circular-fashion conversation.

From Consumer Behaviour to Sourcing

Consumer behaviour eventually becomes a sourcing decision.

If the consumer values comfort, the company must think about:

fabric hand-feel → stretch → construction → fit → supplier capability → quality control

If the consumer values versatility:

multi-occasion design → broader use → product architecture → sourcing flexibility

If the consumer values durability:

material selection → construction → testing → quality assurance → longer potential use

If digital demand is unpredictable:

smaller initial quantities → faster feedback → agile suppliers → replenishment

The consumer may never see these decisions.

But they experience their consequences every time they put the garment on.

The Marketing × Sourcing Matrix

| Consumer signal | Marketing response | Product response | Sourcing implication |
| Comfort | Communicate wear experience | Softness, movement, fit | Fabric and construction quality |
| Fit | Improve size communication | Accurate grading and fit | Supplier consistency |
| Versatility | Show multiple occasions | Multi-use silhouettes | Flexible development |
| Style | Strong visual storytelling | Distinctive design | Design-led sourcing |
| Athleisure | Lifestyle positioning | Performance + everyday design | Technical fabrics |
| Attraction / confidence | Occasion-based styling | Fit, silhouette, finish | Product segmentation |
| Sustainability | Evidence-based communication | Durable/circular design | Traceability |
| Second-hand | Resale/take-back | Design for second life | Reverse logistics |
| Digital demand | Test content quickly | Smaller initial batches | Agile production |
| Everyday staples | Repeat-use positioning | Reliable basics | Stable replenishment |
| Disposal | Repair/take-back | Repairable construction | Reverse logistics |

The matrix demonstrates the central argument of this study:

Consumer research does not stop at marketing.

It travels backwards into the supply chain.

The Netherlands as a Sourcing Lesson for India

The Netherlands is particularly relevant to Indian fashion businesses because India is already part of the Dutch apparel supply chain.

The major apparel suppliers to the Netherlands by import value in 2024 included:

| Country | Share |
| China | 19.9% |
| Germany | 16.1% |
| Bangladesh | 12.0% |
| Türkiye | 8.5% |
| Vietnam | 5.0% |
| Poland | 4.0% |
| India | 3.3% |

For India, the opportunity should not be reduced to producing at a lower price.

The stronger proposition is:

quality + fit + functionality + reliability + compliance + traceability + design + delivery

The Netherlands can therefore be viewed not simply as an export destination, but as a market through which Indian fashion businesses can understand what mature European consumers, retailers and supply chains increasingly expect.

A Quick View of the Dutch Fashion Consumer

| What the research shows | What a fashion business should ask |
| Comfort and fit dominate favourite-garment reasons | Are we designing for actual wear? |
| One in six garments is never worn | What creates wardrobe dormancy? |
| Women own larger wardrobes | Should inventory and communication be segmented differently? |
| Versatility is important | How many situations can one product serve? |
| Digital fashion purchasing is strong | Can online behaviour inform product planning? |
| Sportswear crosses into everyday life | Can performance products become lifestyle products? |
| Circular regulation is strengthening | Is circularity built into the supply chain or added later? |
| Second-hand already exists | Can products be designed for a second life? |
| Clothing has social and situational meaning | Are consumers being segmented only by demographics? |
| Sustainability is not the primary reason for loving a garment | Can sustainability be embedded into the reasons people already value? |

The Bigger Business Insight

The Netherlands demonstrates that fashion consumption is not one behaviour.

It is a sequence of decisions:

•   Context: Where am I going?

•   Comfort: How do I want to feel?

•   Communication: What do I want this outfit to say about me?

•   Convenience: How easily can I find and buy it?

•   Use: Will I actually wear it?

•   Circularity: What happens when I no longer need it?

For fashion businesses, this may be more useful than dividing consumers into simple categories such as “sustainable” or “non-sustainable”.

What can India Learn?

The lesson is not that India should become the Netherlands.

The two markets have different climates, cultures, incomes, consumer structures and fashion traditions.

The lesson is to develop the same discipline of understanding the consumer beyond the transaction.

Five areas stand out:

1. Design for Repeated Use

A garment that works across several situations can create more practical value than one designed only for novelty.

2. Treat Comfort as a Product Strategy

Comfort includes fit, movement, climate, construction, finishing and care.

3. Build Circularity into the Product Lifecycle

Repair, resale, take-back and traceability need to be considered before disposal.

4. Use Digital Behaviour as a Sourcing Signal

AI search, engagement, conversion, reviews and returns can provide demand intelligence.

5. Segment by Situation, Not Only Demographic

A single consumer can represent several different clothing needs across one week.

Her wardrobe is not necessarily one market.

There can be several markets inside one consumer.

What this Means for Future Research

The findings point towards a broader research opportunity around garment retention.

Future primary research could investigate:

•   whether comfort and fit predict repeated use

•   whether novelty accelerates replacement

•   how clothing value changes between work, sport, social, dating and private situations

•   how identity and confidence influence garment retention

•   whether athleisure increases multi-occasion use

•   whether digital and streaming exposure influences purchase and subsequent use

•   how intimate apparel differs from the public wardrobe

•   whether marketing can encourage consumers to retain and repeatedly use garments

•   whether garment retention can become a measurable dimension of circular-fashion strategy

The most important question may ultimately be:

If fashion wants consumers to buy less and use products longer, should the industry focus less on asking consumers to care about sustainability and more on creating products they genuinely want to keep wearing?

That is a question for designers, marketers, sourcing professionals, researchers and policymakers alike.
author: Nithu K
